vignette:
Nadia is a 51-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment after months of resisting the idea that she needed help. She is divorced and works in social ministry, visiting families, organizing support, and meeting parishioners in offices and community rooms where privacy is often part of the job. In the first sessions, what struck her most was how difficult it was to speak plainly about what had happened to her as a child. She could say that a caregiver hurt her physically, but when she tried to go further, her words thinned out and stopped. What came instead was a bodily certainty: her shoulders pulled in, her jaw locked, and she felt herself bracing in the same cramped, defended posture she had been forced into years ago. The memory did not come to her as a story with a beginning and end. It arrived as a position, a surge of rage, and the sense that her body already knew something terrible was happening.

Because the memories came that way, Nadia had built her life around preventing situations in which they might be stirred up. At work she avoided going in when she knew she would need to meet one-on-one behind a closed door, and she had begun canceling or rearranging appointments under practical-sounding excuses. When she did have to be in the building, she chose seats nearest the door and kept herself oriented toward an exit, feeling she had to be able to leave in a second. She also made sure never to be alone with another person if she could help it, asking a colleague to remain nearby or keeping the door open even during conversations that ordinarily required privacy. She understood these habits as necessary because the moment her body started to remember, she no longer trusted herself to stay grounded or safe.

That same bodily remembering also shaped how she moved through ordinary life. A man stepping too close in a hallway, the sound of a chair scraping behind her, or being in a room where someone else controlled the space could bring an immediate jolt. She reacted as if danger were present before she had time to think, turning sharply, checking behind her, scanning for who was there. Her irritability had worsened over the last year; she snapped at coworkers and parishioners with a force that embarrassed her afterward, but in the moment it felt like her whole body had surged into readiness. When memories surfaced, they carried intense rage, and that rage seemed to spill forward into the present, making neutral encounters feel charged and unsafe.

Over time the vigilance began to feed the memories back. At the ministry office, if Nadia caught herself checking the corridor repeatedly or monitoring where everyone was standing, she became more aware of her own tension—arms rigid, back tight, breath held. In those moments she felt herself dropping into the same bodily position she remembered from childhood, and the old scene pressed closer even though she still could not fully narrate it. Her constant sense that something might happen made the past feel near. The more she reacted as though threat were everywhere, the more easily the wordless, physical memory returned.

Her strategies to stay safe narrowed her world, and that narrowing had its own cost. Avoiding workdays, insisting on exits, and refusing to be alone with others gave brief relief, but they also kept her attention fixed on the possibility of danger. Entering a room became an exercise in escape planning. If no easy exit was available, her body tensed immediately; if she could not arrange another person to be present, she felt cornered before anything had happened. Under those conditions she noticed even more false alarms and more compulsive checking behind her. What she called “being careful” left her increasingly on edge, and in that state the old bodily memory was never far away.

The same pattern was now affecting her work in concrete ways. Colleagues had begun covering visits she would once have handled herself, and she worried that people in the ministry were noticing how often she backed out of meetings or positioned herself half-turned toward the door. She hated how quickly anger came into her voice. She especially feared being trapped in a private conversation with a distressed client and suddenly feeling that childhood posture take over her body, along with the rage that accompanied it. What finally brought her in was a recent incident in which a coworker approached from behind while she was setting up a room; Nadia spun around so abruptly and sharply that the coworker recoiled. Nadia was left shaken and ashamed, frightened by how completely the past could overtake the present. She is seeking help now because she wants to keep working and to stop living as if every room contains the same danger, but what frightens her most is the sense that the memory lives in her body beyond words, ready to return whenever she lets her guard down.
